description: We are a team interested in software development and in implementing AI-based solutions. We believe NASA's open data has the potential to help anyone understand changes in the Earth system, and we want to build a tool that turns that information into clear, accessible insights.
summary:
Trend Detective is a web tool for investigating how Earth’s water cycle is changing. It answers the challenge’s core questions (what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant) and adds the one most tools leave open: why.

The tool treats a region’s water like a bank account: the change in stored water equals rain minus evaporation, runoff and human withdrawals. Users choose a region, a time period and a concern, and the tool examines each term with the same statistical method: a Sen trend line, change per decade, a 95% confidence interval and a significance test. Each result is checked against independent sources, such as ground stations, reservoir records and official reports.

The tool delivers a plain-language verdict with its level of certainty, the evidence behind it, and what the data does not say. Every trend is computed in the browser from NASA data (GPM IMERG, GLDAS and GRACE/GRACE-FO) plus other open datasets, so results are transparent and reproducible. An AI assistant answers questions using only the tool’s data and verifies every figure before showing it. This turns satellite data into evidence that citizens, officials and researchers can understand and act on.
details:
Trend Detective, built by team RAACK for “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”, turns a question about environmental change into a case that the reader can investigate. Users choose a region, variables and a period, examine time series, test trends and read a plain-language verdict with its uncertainty and limitations.

HOW THE INVESTIGATION WORKS

Case 001, “Where did the water go?”, treats a region’s water as a budget. It investigates rainfall, temperature, evaporation, soil moisture, runoff, stored water and the possible role of human withdrawals. NASA GPM IMERG, GLDAS and GRACE/GRACE-FO provide the central evidence. CHIRPS, weather records, reservoir observations and official groundwater balances provide independent context. Human withdrawals are not directly measured by this tool.

Each available series shows its trend, change per decade, uncertainty and evidence label. The rate uses Sen’s slope on actual calendar years. Two tests assess the evidence: Mann–Kendall with the Hamed–Rao correction for serial correlation, and least squares with Newey–West errors and a 95% interval. Changing the period recomputes the analysis in the browser. Fixed rules distinguish supply drought, demand drought, compound conditions, a possible human footprint, a one-off dry year and insufficient evidence. Missing observations and inconclusive tests remain visible.

In Nuevo León, the record shows declining stored water alongside a severe dry year in 2022 and official groundwater deficits. The full-record GRACE trend displayed by the tool is approximately −7.1 cm per decade. These observations are consistent with a human footprint; they do not establish causation. A comparison with California’s Central Valley illustrates how the conclusion must weaken when other required evidence is missing.

BEYOND AN ANNUAL TOTAL

Case 002, “Inside the year”, investigates what annual summaries can hide. It compares years with similar rainfall totals but different daily distributions, and provides a guided investigation of rainfall, soil wetness, surface temperature and vegetation across Monterrey.

A globe lets users inspect which of the case’s ten data layers cover a selected country. Where available, it provides a first look at stored water from one GRACE mascon under the country’s reference point. This is neither a countrywide average nor a complete diagnosis.

BENEFITS AND TOOLS

The intended users are citizens, officials, journalists and researchers who need to understand what is changing and assess possible explanations. The creative contribution is a water-budget investigation with the same method across variables, independent witnesses, explicit rules and visible limits, rather than an isolated trend chart. Evidence can inform discussion of responses to a dry year or a persistent water deficit without claiming that statistics establish its cause.

The main application is a static website built with Svelte, TypeScript, Vite and d3 modules. It computes trends in the browser from data files prepared from the source records. Python scripts and reference calculations support reproducibility; tests in the repository compare the browser engine with pymannkendall and statsmodels. The interface supports English and Spanish, desktop and phone, light and dark themes, and reduced motion.

DE-T is an optional AI assistant powered by Kimi from Moonshot AI. It uses tools to retrieve or calculate information from the project’s own records, and a checker flags numerical values it cannot match. It appears only while the team enables its separate backend; the static investigations work independently. Real-model server tests are documented, while a complete public browser interaction with the real model remains unverified. Matching a number does not verify the surrounding interpretation.

LIMITATIONS AND CREDITS

GRACE cannot separate groundwater from soil, reservoirs or ice; GLDAS is a model; official groundwater availability is an administrative balance; and statistical significance does not establish a cause. The second case’s map contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025) through NASA’s Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 imagery. Source data, methods, software and visual credits are documented in the repository. This is not an official NASA product.

USE OF AI

During preparation, Claude produced possible features for discussion; these suggestions were not team decisions. Team members defined the selected water-budget investigation, its scientific method and verdict rules. Fran proposed the questions behind the second case and the country-coverage exploration.

Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted with research, data preparation and analysis, code, debugging, automated tests, interface design, documentation, translation and submission drafts under the team’s direction. AI also helped identify and correct a slope calculation that treated missing years as consecutive observations. The repository preserves the comparison and corrected calculation.

DE-T uses Kimi inside the product to generate explanations from the project’s records and computational tools. Its numerical checker does not guarantee that an explanation is correct. Scientific observations come from the cited providers, rather than synthetic observations generated by AI. No AI-generated imagery or audio is reported in the current project documentation.
